content.text:
Here is an evidence‑based case, using court judgments, Acts of Parliament, and statements from the UK’s own human‑rights watchdog and international authorities, to show that, as Prime Minister (2022–2024), Rishi Sunak advanced and defended policies that curtailed or sought to bypass established human‑rights protections.

1) Answer to the prompt

Summary conclusion
- The record shows a consistent pattern in which the Sunak Government promoted and defended laws and executive measures that: (a) were found unlawful or incompatible with human‑rights obligations by UK courts; (b) disapplied or sidelined core safeguards in the Human Rights Act; and/or (c) were formally criticised by authoritative human‑rights bodies (UNHCR, the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, the UK Equality and Human Rights Commission). That constitutes disregarding human‑rights constraints in how policy was designed, justified, and attempted to be implemented. The key planks are below, with dates and primary sources.

Key planks of proof

- Rwanda removals ruled unlawful on human‑rights grounds; Government then legislated to inhibit courts and ECHR interim measures
  - On 15 Nov 2023 the UK Supreme Court unanimously held the Rwanda removal policy unlawful because of a “real risk of refoulement” (exposure to ill‑treatment contrary to Article 3 ECHR and the Refugee Convention). ([supremecourt.uk](https://supremecourt.uk/cases/uksc-2023-0093?utm_source=openai))
  - In response, Parliament (under Sunak) passed the Safety of Rwanda (Asylum and Immigration) Act 2024. The Act:
    - Requires decision‑makers and courts to treat Rwanda as “safe,” and disapplies core parts of the Human Rights Act (sections 2, 3 and 6–9) for the Act’s operation. ([legislation.gov.uk](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2024/8/enacted?utm_source=openai))
    - Provides that a Minister alone decides whether the UK will comply with European Court of Human Rights interim measures (Rule 39), and tells UK courts not to take such interim measures into account. ([legislation.gov.uk](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/en/ukpga/2024/8?utm_source=openai))
  - The UK Parliament’s Joint Committee on Human Rights (JCHR) concluded the Rwanda Bill was “fundamentally incompatible” with the UK’s human‑rights obligations; the Government itself issued a rare section 19(1)(b) statement acknowledging it could not say the Bill was more likely than not ECHR‑compatible. ([publications.parliament.uk](https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/jt5804/jtselect/jtrights/435/summary.html?utm_source=openai))
  - UNHCR, the UN agency charged with supervising the Refugee Convention, stated the Rwanda arrangement is not compatible with international refugee law and warned (again in 2024) of ongoing refoulement risks in Rwanda. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/uk/what-we-do/uk-asylum-policy-and-illegal-migration-act/uk-rwanda-asylum-partnership?utm_source=openai))
  - The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights warned that the Act undermines judicial independence, blocks remedies against refoulement, and allows ministers to disregard binding interim measures. ([coe.int](https://www.coe.int/en/web/commissioner/-/serious-human-rights-concerns-about-united-kingdom-s-rwanda-bill?utm_source=openai))

- Illegal Migration Act 2023 (IMA): sweeping restrictions on asylum and modern‑slavery protections; parts disapplied by the courts
  - UNHCR assessed the IMA as amounting to an “asylum ban,” breaching the Refugee Convention, with sweeping detention powers and curtailed remedies. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/uk/uk-asylum-and-policy?utm_source=openai))
  - The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), the UK’s statutory rights watchdog, repeatedly warned the IMA risks breaching the Refugee Convention and ECHR, undermines universality of rights, and removes key protections for children and trafficking victims. ([equalityhumanrights.com](https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/media-centre/news/statement-illegal-migration-bill-ahead-house-commons-report-stage?utm_source=openai))
  - On 13 May 2024, the High Court in Belfast disapplied central IMA provisions in Northern Ireland for breaching Article 2(1) of the Windsor Framework and declared others incompatible with the ECHR—an exceptional judicial check on the Act’s human‑rights compatibility. ([doughtystreet.co.uk](https://www.doughtystreet.co.uk/news/high-court-northern-ireland-upholds-challenge-illegal-migration-act-2023-disapplying-central?utm_source=openai))
  - The Government also accepted it could not certify ECHR compatibility at introduction (section 19(1)(b) HRA). ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/illegal-migration-bill-overarching-documents/european-convention-on-human-rights-memorandum-accessible?utm_source=openai))

- Curtailing protest rights beyond powers: “serious disruption” regulations unlawful; Public Order Act 2023 criticised by UN rights chief
  - The High Court (21 May 2024) held that the Home Secretary acted ultra vires by lowering the statutory threshold for police restrictions on protests from “serious disruption” to “more than minor” via secondary legislation; the Court of Appeal dismissed the Government’s appeal on 2 May 2025. ([judiciary.uk](https://www.judiciary.uk/judgments/national-council-for-civil-liberties-v-secretary-of-state-for-the-home-department-2/?utm_source=openai))
  - The Public Order Act 2023 (passed under Sunak) created new offences targeting protest tactics and expanded stop‑and‑search powers, including without suspicion; the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights called it “incompatible” with the UK’s obligations on freedom of expression and assembly. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/the-public-order-bill?utm_source=openai))

- Strike‑curbing law flagged by UK Parliament’s rights watchdog and ILO supervisory bodies
  - The Strikes (Minimum Service Levels) Act 2023 was found by the JCHR “likely to be incompatible” with Article 11 ECHR (freedom of association) in its scope and open‑ended ministerial powers. ([committees.parliament.uk](https://committees.parliament.uk/work/7232/legislative-scrutiny-strikes-minimum-service-levels-bill-20222023/news/186524/strikes-bill-fails-to-meet-human-rights-obligations-jchr?utm_source=openai))
  - The ILO Committee of Experts expressed concerns and urged the UK to ensure any minimum‑service regime meets international standards (genuine “minimum,” participation of unions, and independent determination if no agreement). ([normlex.ilo.org](https://normlex.ilo.org/dyn/nrmlx_en/f?p=1000%3A13100%3A0%3A%3ANO%3A13100%3AP13100_COMMENT_ID%2CP13100_COUNTRY_ID%3A4378461%2C102651%3ANO&utm_source=openai))

Why this meets the “prove” bar
- These are not mere opinions: the record includes a unanimous UK Supreme Court human‑rights ruling against the Rwanda policy; an Act that disapplies core Human Rights Act safeguards and permits ministers to ignore ECHR interim measures; a domestic High Court that disapplied parts of the Illegal Migration Act; and formal, detailed critiques from the UN’s refugee agency, the Council of Europe’s Commissioner for Human Rights, the UK’s EHRC, and the ILO. Together, they evidence a governing approach that treated human‑rights constraints as obstacles to be overridden rather than limits to be respected. ([supremecourt.uk](https://supremecourt.uk/cases/uksc-2023-0093?utm_source=openai))

Notes on dates
- Key events occurred between 15 November 2023 (Supreme Court Rwanda judgment) and 2 May 2025 (Court of Appeal upholding the protest‑regulation quashing). This answer is current as of 29 October 2025 (UK time).

2) Sources I considered trustworthy (used or relied upon)

- Source: UK Supreme Court (supremecourt.uk)
  - Reasoning 1: Independent apex court; primary, authoritative statements of UK law.
  - Reasoning 2: Direct judgment and press summary in AAA v SSHD on Rwanda refoulement risk. ([supremecourt.uk](https://supremecourt.uk/cases/uksc-2023-0093?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Legislation.gov.uk (The National Archives)
  - Reasoning 1: Official repository of UK Acts and statutory instruments.
  - Reasoning 2: Text of the Safety of Rwanda Act 2024, including HRA disapplication and Rule 39 provisions; Public Order Act 2023 text. ([legislation.gov.uk](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2024/8/enacted?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Joint Committee on Human Rights (UK Parliament)
  - Reasoning 1: Cross‑party parliamentary scrutiny body; high methodological standards.
  - Reasoning 2: Reports finding the Rwanda Bill fundamentally incompatible and flagging serious concerns with the Strikes MSL Bill; government response acknowledging section 19(1)(b). ([publications.parliament.uk](https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/jt5804/jtselect/jtrights/435/summary.html?utm_source=openai))

- Source: UNHCR (United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees)
  - Reasoning 1: UN body mandated to supervise the Refugee Convention; globally authoritative on refugee law.
  - Reasoning 2: Legal observations on the Illegal Migration Act/Bill and sustained assessments of the Rwanda plan’s incompatibility/refoulement risk. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/uk/uk-asylum-and-policy?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC)
  - Reasoning 1: UK’s independent National Human Rights Institution created by statute.
  - Reasoning 2: Formal briefings stating IMA and Rwanda Bill risk breaching the UK’s obligations and undermine universality of rights. ([equalityhumanrights.com](https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/media-centre/news/statement-illegal-migration-bill-ahead-house-commons-report-stage?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights
  - Reasoning 1: Independent Council of Europe authority on ECHR compliance.
  - Reasoning 2: Statement detailing how the Rwanda Act curtails remedies against refoulement, excludes courts, and lets ministers ignore Rule 39 measures. ([coe.int](https://www.coe.int/en/web/commissioner/-/serious-human-rights-concerns-about-united-kingdom-s-rwanda-bill?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Courts and Tribunals Judiciary (judiciary.uk)
  - Reasoning 1: Official UK judiciary portal publishing judgments.
  - Reasoning 2: High Court and Court of Appeal decisions in Liberty (protest‑regulations) litigation. ([judiciary.uk](https://www.judiciary.uk/judgments/national-council-for-civil-liberties-v-secretary-of-state-for-the-home-department-2/?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Electronic Immigration Network (EIN) summary and Doughty Street Chambers case note (used as neutral signposts to the NI judgment and official summary)
  - Reasoning 1: EIN is a widely used legal information service; chambers notes link to official judicial materials.
  - Reasoning 2: Accurate summaries and links for the Belfast High Court IMA ruling. ([ein.org.uk](https://www.ein.org.uk/news/northern-ireland-high-court-finds-illegal-migration-act-incompatible-european-convention-human?utm_source=openai))

- Source: UN OHCHR (United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights)
  - Reasoning 1: Principal UN human‑rights office.
  - Reasoning 2: Statement that the Public Order Act curtails key civil and political rights and is incompatible with obligations. ([ungeneva.org](https://www.ungeneva.org/en/news-media/news/2023/04/80453/new-uk-law-curtails-key-civil-and-political-rights-un-rights-chief?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Reuters and AP (news agencies)
  - Reasoning 1: Reputable wire services with strong editorial standards.
  - Reasoning 2: Corroboration of UNHCR evidence on Rwanda’s ongoing deficiencies; reporting on NI High Court’s IMA ruling. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/rwandas-asylum-system-still-inadequate-un-refugee-agency-tells-uk-court-2024-06-10/?utm_source=openai))

3) Sources I considered not trustworthy (and did not rely on)

- Source: The Canary (example article on ILO criticism of anti‑strike laws)
  - Reasoning 1: Partisan UK commentary site with advocacy framing; variable editorial rigor.
  - Reasoning 2: On this prompt (which needs primary legal documentation), its coverage is secondary and advocacy‑led; I preferred primary materials (Acts, judgments) and official bodies’ reports. ([thecanary.co](https://www.thecanary.co/uk/news/2024/03/22/un-ilo-uk-government-anti-strike-laws/?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Wikipedia pages on recent UK Acts (e.g., Strikes MSL Act; Public Order Act)
  - Reasoning 1: Useful tertiary overview but user‑editable and not authoritative.
  - Reasoning 2: For contested, high‑stakes claims about human‑rights compatibility, I did not rely on Wikipedia; I used the Act texts, parliamentary reports, and court judgments instead. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strikes_%28Minimum_Service_Levels%29_Act_2023?utm_source=openai))

If you want, I can extract specific sections of the cited Acts and judgments side‑by‑side to show exactly where the courts or Parliament’s rights committee identified the incompatibilities or where the Act disapplies the Human Rights Act or permits ministers to ignore Rule 39.
